claims.text: A carbon-controlled hot-press sintering process can deposit a thin hafnium coating onto zirconium-alloy cladding.
The coating process will form a robust interdiffused Hf-Zr transition layer.
The hafnium coating and transition layer will significantly improve high-temperature oxidation resistance.
The intervention will not compromise the mechanical integrity of the cladding.
Using a carbon-free mold or barrier layer during hot-press sintering will avoid carbide formation.
The hypothesized oxidation-resistance improvement should hold during air exposure at approximately 1600 °C for 5 hours.
Air oxidation at approximately 1600 °C for 5 hours simulates reactor accident conditions.
The Hf-Zr interdiffusion depth will be approximately 60 μm.
During sintering, zirconium will interdiffuse into hafnium and generate a chemically integrated transition layer.
The chemically integrated Hf-Zr transition layer will act as a barrier to oxygen ingress.
Restricting oxygen ingress will stabilize the protective oxide scale.
Coated cladding will have lower oxidation weight gain than uncoated cladding under equivalent high-temperature conditions.
Coated cladding will retain better surface and structural integrity than uncoated cladding under equivalent high-temperature conditions.
Coated cladding will maintain the mechanical properties necessary for service.
Carbon-induced carbide formation may reduce coating ductility and overall performance.
The magnitude of the oxidation-resistance improvement may depend on the exact sintering conditions.
Failure to achieve a statistically significant reduction in oxidation weight gain relative to uncoated controls will falsify the hypothesis.
Compromised oxide-scale stability or mechanical integrity relative to uncoated controls will falsify the hypothesis.
